topics: Console: JSON-mode editor, contract validation, and sandboxed tool invokes
Runtime failover and fallback policies (model variant routing)
Compliance: KMS, audit logs, VPC/private deployment
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-02 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Li (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Ellen Shaw (Northern Labs Head of ML), Marcus Yu (Platform Eng), Sofia Alvarez (Security Lead), Tom Benson (PM)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll run the demo in about 50 minutes or so, show the runbook flow, JSON-mode payloads, and how the runtime handles fallback. Quick intro round robin?

[00:15] Ellen: Ellen, hi. We're looking to standardize how our chat assistant calls backend tools and to avoid those... um, inconsistent outputs we've been seeing. Marcus will handle infra questions.

[00:27] Marcus: Marcus here, yeah mainly concerned about VPC and latency as we have 50ms SLO on some queries.

[00:34] Jordan: Great, thanks. Priya, do you want to kick off the screen?

[00:40] Priya: Yup, sharing now. Alright, console up — this is the JSON-mode editor, so you can see a typed contract on the left, sample payloads in the middle, and the sandbox invoke on the right. We'll step through a runbook that extracts user intent, validates against a schema and then calls an order-lookup tool.

[01:05] Tom: Quick question, is the schema enforcement runtime or pre-commit? Like, do we get hard rejections at runtime?

[01:12] Priya: Good question. There are two layers — compile-time validation in the console so engineers see issues when authoring, and at runtime the service validates the final JSON payload before tool invoke. If the payload fails, you get a structured error with a fallback path.

[01:30] Ellen: So that fallback could trigger a lower-latency, smaller model rather than erroring out?

[01:35] Priya: Exactly. We showed model-variant routing where a policy can route to a cheaper quantized model, or a cached response if a matching prefix exists.

[02:02] Marcus: What's the KV cache behavior? If I call the same tool with same context, how does prefix matching work?

[02:08] Priya: We do prefix/KV caching at token granularity, it's workload aware. In practice for your top 10 intents you'll see up to 4x token cost reduction depending on hit rate. But caches TTLs and scope are configurable per-route.

[02:35] Jordan: I want to show a live runbook now. In this flow the model outputs a typed action: {"action": "lookup_order", "order_id": "string"}. The console validates that order_id matches the regex, then calls the internal order service via a sandboxed tool. Watch the validation errors pop if we send bad input.

[03:10] Priya: Alright, invoking with a malformed order id... you can see the red validation marker — the runtime returned a structured failure, we then show the human escalation step configured in the runbook.

[03:38] Sofia: Pause — is the tool invocation proxied through Redwood or does it run in the customer's VPC?

[03:45] Priya: Two options: hosted mode where calls are proxied and sanitized, or Private (VPC) where the customer provides an egress gateway and the tool endpoints are called from within the customer's network. For regulated data we recommend VPC/private.

[04:05] Sofia: For us, all PII must stay in VPC and keys controlled by our KMS. How do you support HSM or external KMS?

[04:12] Jordan: We integrate with customer KMS systems and can support wrapped keys/HSM-backed KMS for Private deployments. We'll share our compliance pack.

[04:28] Priya: Back to the runbook — next I'm going to show failover. We simulate the order service being slow. Notice the runbook policy: if tool latency > 200ms, route to a cached path or return summary and open a ticket.

[04:50] [05:00] (brief pause while Priya toggles network sim)

[05:10] Priya: Triggering slow response... the runtime detected tail latency and executed the fallback: first attempt to cached KV, second, a cheaper model for a paraphrase answer, third, escalate to human. Logs show trace id and per-token timing.

[06:02] Marcus: That trace id, can we push it into our observability stack? Datadog or Splunk?

[06:08] Priya: Yes — we emit spans and logs to your configured sink. You can get token-level latency metrics per route and per model.

[06:25] Ellen: In terms of evals, can we assert semantic parity between primary and fallback model outputs?

[06:32] Priya: We have quality monitoring hooks; you can attach prompt sets and ground truth and we alert on regressions. For fallbacks you can set acceptance thresholds so the fallback only returns if it meets a confidence score.

[07:00] Jordan: Switching to API demo: here's the same runbook invoked via the REST API. You POST the user message and a runbook_id, and the response includes typed JSON or an error object.

[07:16] Marcus: How large are these responses? Do they include full token streams?

[07:20] Priya: Response can be streaming or final. For typed actions we usually return a compact JSON payload — the console can also stream structured patches if you want partial results.

[07:45] Tom: What about rate limits? Our busiest endpoints hit bursts of 2k reqs per second seasonally.

[07:52] Jordan: For Dedicated or Private you can provision reserved capacity and autoscale rules; SLAs are backed by throughput tiers. For hosted, we have burst quotas and recommend Dedicated for sustained high qps. We'll include example pricing tiers in the pilot doc.

[08:18] Ellen: Security again — will Redwood be able to see raw messages in hosted mode? We need clarity for legal.

[08:25] Jordan: In hosted, metadata and telemetry are visible; payload retention is configurable per-account. For strict compliance, Private deployment keeps all traffic in your VPC and we only manage control plane metadata. We'll send the exact retention options.

[09:00] Priya: Now I'll demo the failover policy in the runbook editor. You can edit priority, add matchers on latency or error codes, and preview simulated executions with synthetic traces.

[09:32] [09:55] Priya: Simulating a model variant fallback — see how we can route to a 4-bit quantized variant for cheap reads. The console shows estimated cost delta and latency impact.

[10:12] Marcus: Curious — how do you validate the quantized variant's semantic fidelity?

[10:20] Priya: We run A/B evals and holdout prompts; the Optimize tool suggests quantization levels per workload. For critical paths you can block auto-fallback unless manual approval is given.

[10:50] Ellen: For the pilot we want to measure p95 and p99 latencies and also token cost. Can Redwood export cost breakdowns per route?

[10:58] Jordan: Yes — Console and API both give per-route and per-token cost breakdowns. We'll attach a sample cost analysis sheet for your workload.

[11:20] Tom: A hypothetical — if the typed action fails schema at runtime, can we return a best-effort human-friendly message instead of raw error?

[11:28] Priya: Yes, runbook can map structured failures to UX messages, or trigger a correction flow where the model attempts a repair with a constrained prompt.

[11:45] [12:05] Ellen: Are there any known gotchas when connecting to internal services through the private egress?

[12:11] Marcus: We did a quick trial with another vendor and had NAT session limits cause issues; do you support connection pooling or edge proxies?

[12:20] Priya: We recommend an egress gateway with connection pooling. For Private we instrument keepalives and reuse TLS sessions; we'll share an ops runbook for network tuning.

[12:40] Jordan: I'm going to show a small failure scenario chain — bad schema -> fallback to cached -> cheaper model -> human escalation. This demonstrates graceful degradation without exposing raw stack traces.

[13:05] Priya: Executing synthetic prompt now... and you can see in the audit log the structured entries: runbook_id, trace_id, route chosen, model name, fallback reason. All of that is queryable.

[13:35] Sofia: How long are audit logs retained? We need at least 1 year for some audits.

[13:40] Jordan: Retention is configurable; default is 90 days on hosted, but enterprise packages can extend to 1+ year with additional storage.

[14:05] Tom: Any pointer on network egress cost when doing Private? We pay for cross-region traffic.

[14:12] Priya: We can pin regions and provide capacity in the same cloud region to minimize egress. We'll also show cost modeling for peak traffic.

[14:40] [15:00] Marcus: Will you be able to support our existing auth? We use SAML SSO and service-to-service JWTs.

[15:07] Jordan: SSO for console is SAML/OIDC, API keys for programmatic access, and we support short-lived service tokens for inter-service calls. For Private we recommend mutual TLS to the egress gateway.

[15:30] Ellen: Could you walk through a sample JSON response from the runbook when everything succeeds?

[15:36] Priya: Sure — sample: {"action":"lookup_order","order_id":"ORD-1234","result":{"status":"shipped","eta":"2026-07-05"}} — that's what the runtime returns. If there is a validation warning we also include a warnings array.

[16:10] Tom: Do we get a canonical schema artifact we can check into our repo?

[16:15] Priya: Yes — console exports JSON Schema files and a versioned catalog; runbook ids map to schema versions so you can pin behavior.

[16:40] Jordan: demo note — as part of the pilot we'll propose a small commit for 2 reserved GPUs and a 48-hour test with SANDBOX data.

[17:00] Ellen: For data handling, can we scrub PII before it hits Redwood in hosted mode?

[17:06] Priya: You can configure pre-send sanitizers in the SDK or use an inline scrubber in the runbook before any outbound tools.

[17:25] Marcus: About latency again — we talked p95 but our SLA needs p50 under 60ms for queries served from cache. Is that achievable?

[17:33] Priya: For cache hits yes; end-to-end depends on network hop and your egress setup. In our tests p50 cache-hit times were typically sub-30ms on dedicated infra. We'll model this with your traces.

[18:00] Jordan: Okay, switching to a mini technical deep dive: how the runtime validates typed payloads — we use a two-stage approach: light-weight preflight in GRPC boundary and a strict validator inside the worker process. That reduces false positives on high-throughput routes.

[18:32] Ellen: Does that add significant overhead?

[18:36] Priya: Minimal — validation is optimized and can be skipped for non-critical routes. The overhead is <2ms in our benchmarks per request for typical schemas.

[19:00] [20:00] (brief back-and-forth about internal deployment diagrams; Priya shares architecture)

[20:30] Priya: Now I'll show the Optimize tab — it suggests quantization levels, batching windows, and cache TTLs based on your traffic pattern. You can accept suggestions or run a simulated cost run.

[20:55] Marcus: If we accept automated batching increases, does that risk increased tail latency for interactive sessions?

[21:02] Priya: Optimize balances latency SLO and cost; you can set a hard latency floor and Optimize will only suggest configs that maintain it. Also, can set per-route exceptions for interactive flows.

[21:30] Tom: For the pilot, can we have a canary rollout so not all users hit the new runbook?

[21:36] Jordan: Yes — canary percentage, A/B routing, and auto-fallback are built-in. We'll include a recommended rollout plan in the pilot doc.

[22:05] Ellen: On legal, we need to know what the shared responsibility is for data breaches.

[22:12] Jordan: We'll give you the SLA and security responsibility matrix. For Private deployments Redwood's exposure is limited to the control plane, but we'll have formal language in the contract.

[22:40] Priya: Quick demo of the sandboxed tool runner — this simulates calling your internal microservice with request/response redaction. We can show live request logs with masked fields.

[23:08] Sofia: Can we control the masking rules? e.g., mask email, but keep order id unmasked?

[23:14] Priya: Yes, masking is rule-based and pluggable. You define patterns or use an allowlist.

[23:35] [25:00] (mini Q&A; Jordan clarifies pricing buckets and we note action items)

[25:25] Jordan: To recap — pilot scope: 2-week onboarding, 48-hour load test, runbook templates, and compliance docs. Delivery: pilot proposal by Jordan, runbook examples by Priya.

[25:45] Ellen: That matches our expectation, I'd add security checklist and sample contract redlines.

[26:00] Marcus: We'll also provide sample traces and a service endpoint for the private egress.

[26:15] Priya: We'll need credentials for the sandbox; we'll supply a provisioning guide.

[27:00] Tom: Any blockers from legal on your side?

[27:05] Jordan: None immediate, but we'll need to loop in contracts once scope is finalized.

[27:30] [28:00] (small tangent about competitor feature parity; mentions Anthropic, OpenAI and homegrown runtimes)

[28:35] Sofia: One more security item — audit logs must include redaction proof for PII. Is that possible?

[28:42] Priya: We maintain redaction hashes and a redaction proof log; auditors can verify that PII was scrubbed at ingestion time. We'll detail this in the security pack.

[29:10] Jordan: Time check — we have about half the meeting left, want to go deeper on any area?

[29:18] Ellen: Let's do a quick run through of the failure modes and playground a couple of edge cases.

[29:25] Priya: Sure — I'll open the failure-case runner. Example 1: schema mismatch then auto-repair attempt. Example 2: tool times out and fallback to cached summary. Example 3: model produces invalid type so runbook requests a correction via a constrained prompt.

[30:00] [31:00] Priya: Running example 1 — the model responded with order id as number instead of string; the repair prompt converted and validated — you then see the corrected typed-action displayed and the tool invoked.

[31:40] Marcus: That's neat; what's the best way to handle partial successes? e.g., some fields missing but non-blocking?

[31:46] Priya: Runbooks support optional fields and you can configure soft-warnings. The UI surfaces warnings and the response includes a partial payload with a warnings array.

[32:10] Tom: For telemetry, can we attach business metrics like revenue impact to a route?

[32:15] Jordan: You can annotate routes with arbitrary tags and push that to cost/quality dashboards — good for correlating cost to business value.

[33:00] [34:00] (demo continues showing console export of schema and a sample SDK call)

[34:30] Priya: Now I'm invoking the API with a streaming response to show partial typed output and patch updates. You can see the patch diffs in the UI.

[34:55] Ellen: In the streaming case, can downstream services handle partial typed actions?

[35:02] Priya: We recommend only final payloads for critical tool calls; streaming is great for UX but for tool invocation we buffer until contract validated.

[35:40] Marcus: How often do you release runtime patches? We have strict change windows.

[35:45] Jordan: For Private we can align maintenance windows; hosted has regular releases with optional opt-in for major changes. We'll provide an upgrade schedule.

[36:10] Tom: Onboarding timeline if we say yes to pilot next week?

[36:15] Jordan: Typical is 2 weeks for initial setup and 1-2 weeks for pilot runs; we'll tailor.

[36:40] Priya: Final mini demo — showing a degraded network where model calls cross region, runtime routes to local replica and using cached responses where appropriate.

[37:05] Ellen: Looks promising. For the pilot, can we validate the A/B parity between primary and fallback? We need to show no regression on critical prompts.

[37:12] Priya: We'll set up holdout prompt sets and automated evaluation; Optimize will surface regression deltas.

[37:40] [40:00] (discussion on legal/commercial timelines and pilot acceptance criteria)

[40:30] Jordan: Ok I'll summarize the ask: deliver pilot proposal, security docs, console recording, runbook examples, and schedule the 48-hour load window.

[40:50] Marcus: We'll send sample traces and the service endpoint, and Sofia will send compliance constraints.

[41:10] Ellen: Any final questions?

[41:15] Tom: One small ask — can we get a sample contract clause for data residency?

[41:20] Jordan: Yes, we'll include a sample clause in the pilot package.

[41:40] Priya: I'll follow up with a short how-to for the private egress setup and a checklist for masking rules.

[42:05] [43:00] (wrap-up, Jordan restates next steps aloud)

[43:10] Jordan: Recap quick: Jordan sends pilot pricing + sample SLA, Priya shares runbook and console clip, Sofia provides compliance items, Marcus provides traces. We'll reconvene after pilot scoping.

[43:40] Ellen: Sounds good, thanks everyone.

[43:50] Jordan: Thank you — we'll follow up by email.

[44:00] (meeting ends, informal chatter for a minute)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hear of acronyms, some filler words and overlapping talk captured.
